title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana's land loss has slowed, so the crisis is over

Rebuttal: It's true USGS found the rate slowed. But USGS said the main reason was probably no major hurricane hitting the wetlands from 2008 to 2016. That's luck. The state's own 2023 Master Plan still projects 1,100 to 3,000 more square miles lost by 2070 without action.

Sources: USGS, 2017, Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Oil and gas canals had nothing to do with Louisiana's land loss

Rebuttal: Other causes matter too: river levees, subsidence, storms. But a federal study for the Minerals Management Service tied canals and spoil banks to at least 30 to 60 percent of wetland loss from 1955 to 1978. The industry wasn't the only cause. It was a big one.

Sources: Minerals Management Service-sponsored study, 1987, LSU, 2022

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Canceling the Mid-Barataria diversion saved Louisiana's fishing industry

Rebuttal: Fishers had real reasons to fear it, especially oyster harvesters. But canceling it didn't stop the land from sinking, and the coast that shelters nurseries for shrimp and fish keeps shrinking. The state's own plan warns of major losses without big land-building. The answer is a plan that pays fishers fairly and still builds land.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025, Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The Mid-Barataria diversion was a waste of taxpayer money

Rebuttal: Costs did climb and the project faced lawsuits. But the money was mostly BP settlement funds meant for coastal restoration, not general taxes. The waste is canceling after authorizing more than $600 million without a replacement plan.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025, U.S. Department of Justice, 2015

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The Coastal Master Plan is too expensive to fund

Rebuttal: $50 billion over 50 years is real money. But the plan estimates up to $15 billion a year in damage without action by 2070. Spending about $1 billion a year to prevent up to $15 billion a year in losses is a bargain.

Sources: Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan, WWNO, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Sea level rise is too slow to matter in our lifetime

Rebuttal: Globally the rise is gradual. But on the Louisiana coast, sinking land makes it fast. NOAA's Grand Isle gauge shows about 9 millimeters a year, around 3 feet a century. That's within a mortgage, not a millennium.

Sources: NOAA Tides and Currents, USGS, 2017

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The Gulf dead zone is a natural phenomenon

Rebuttal: Low oxygen can happen naturally in places. But the Gulf dead zone is driven by nutrient runoff down the Mississippi, which is why a federal task force set a goal to shrink it. The 2025 five-year average was about 4,755 square miles, versus a goal of under 1,900.

Sources: NOAA, 2025, Hypoxia Task Force

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The dead zone was smaller in 2025, so the problem is solved

Rebuttal: 2025 was below average at about 4,402 square miles, and that's good. But size swings with rainfall and river flow. The five-year average is still more than double the target. One mild year isn't a policy win.

Sources: NOAA, 2025, UPI, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Dropping the Denka case was about respecting the law, not abandoning communities

Rebuttal: The government argued the case overreached, and Denka has denied its emissions endangered residents. But EPA itself filed the case in 2023 over cancer risk near homes. Then in 2025, 12 Louisiana plants, including Denka, got exemptions from new air toxics limits. The pattern points one way.

Sources: Manufacturing Dive, 2025, Louisiana Illuminator, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The HON rule exemptions protect American manufacturing jobs

Rebuttal: Compliance does cost money. But the rule targets cancer-causing chemicals like ethylene oxide near neighborhoods. Twelve Louisiana plants got two-year passes. Workers in those plants breathe the same air as their neighbors. Clean air protects workers too.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025, EPA, 2024 HON rule

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The Formosa plant will bring jobs St. James desperately needs

Rebuttal: St. James needs jobs, that's true. But the project has been stalled for years, the Army Corps ordered a full environmental review, and a 2025 IEEFA analysis told Formosa to walk away because the plastics market is oversupplied. A plant that may never be built is not a jobs plan.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025, IEEFA, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Risk Rating 2.0 just made flood insurance fair

Rebuttal: Pricing risk more accurately has merit. But in Louisiana about 52,000 people dropped coverage and 80 percent of policyholders saw increases. A fair price nobody can pay leaves more homes uninsured and more people needing disaster aid later.

Sources: Office of U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy, 2024, FEMA NFIP

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana homeowners just need to shop around for cheaper insurance

Rebuttal: Shopping can help some. But a standard policy averaged about $5,400 in 2024, and up to $14,400 in parts of the south. Many insurers left after the 2020 and 2021 storms. You can't shop in a market that walked out.

Sources: Climate and Community Institute, 2025, Louisiana Illuminator, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Paying insurers incentives fixed Louisiana's insurance market

Rebuttal: The incentive program did move tens of thousands of policies out of Citizens. But premiums stayed among the highest in America, and 59 percent of homeowners would pay more than a tenth of income for standard coverage. Paying companies to come back isn't the same as making insurance affordable.

Sources: Insurance Journal, 2024, Climate and Community Institute, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: FEMA's BRIC program was wasteful and needed to go

Rebuttal: BRIC was slow; only about 21.6 percent of FY2020 to FY2023 selections had been obligated by 2026. That's a reason to fix it, not kill it. A federal court ruled the termination unlawful in December 2025. Louisiana had about $721 million in projects at stake.

Sources: Congressional Research Service, 2026, WWNO, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: States should handle disaster prevention on their own

Rebuttal: States do play a lead role. But Louisiana can't raise the money for big drainage and grid projects alone, and storms don't respect budgets. When BRIC ended, projects in Baton Rouge, Ascension and New Orleans stalled. Federal help is what a union of states is for.

Sources: WWNO, 2025, WAFB, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Hurricane deaths are mostly from flooding, so heat protections don't matter after storms

Rebuttal: Water is deadly, no question. But in Louisiana, many early Ida deaths came after the storm: at least 10 from heat and 6 from carbon monoxide by mid-September 2021. Power loss is a killer. Backup power and cooling save lives.

Sources: Louisiana Department of Health, 2021, Louisiana Illuminator, 2021

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Nursing homes know best how to evacuate their own residents

Rebuttal: Most operators do try. But during Ida about 800 nursing home residents were moved into one warehouse, and residents died after that evacuation. Self-policing failed. Plans need inspection and enforcement.

Sources: EMS1, 2021, Associated Press, 2021

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Heat deaths are rare and exaggerated

Rebuttal: Heat deaths are smaller than heart disease, sure. But CDC counted 2,391 heat-related deaths in 2024, and the largest share were people 65 to 74. That's more than six a day. Many experts say official counts likely miss cases.

Sources: CDC, NCHS, 2026, EPA heat deaths indicator documentation

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Fossil fuels aren't subsidized, they pay taxes like everyone else

Rebuttal: Oil and gas companies do pay taxes. But the IMF counted about $1.3 trillion in explicit fossil fuel subsidies worldwide in 2022, things like price controls and rebates. Counting unpaid pollution damage as implicit subsidy, the total was about $7 trillion. Both are costs the public carries.

Sources: IMF, 2023, Fortune, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Clean energy tax credits were handouts to rich people

Rebuttal: Some benefits did go to higher earners, like early EV buyers. But the credits also paid for wind and solar that now make up nearly 54 percent of power generation jobs. Ending the home solar credit after 2025 hits working families trying to lower their bills.

Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, 2025 USEER, Kirkland & Ellis, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Clean energy jobs are a fantasy

Rebuttal: Many clean energy jobs are newer and some pay less than union oil jobs. That's a fight worth having. But DOE counted about 8.5 million energy jobs in 2024, and wind and solar were nearly 54 percent of power generation jobs. The jobs are real. The question is pay and who gets them.

Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, 2025 USEER, Industrial Info, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: LNG exports are the future of Louisiana's economy

Rebuttal: LNG is huge: the U.S. is the top exporter at about 15 billion cubic feet a day in 2025, much of it from Louisiana. But construction booms fade into small permanent crews. The Data Center found Louisiana job growth under 1 percent over a dozen years even through the boom.

Sources: EIA, via Journal of Petroleum Technology, 2026, The Data Center, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana's economy depends on oil and gas, so we can't change

Rebuttal: Oil and gas matter here; an industry study says it's a big share of the state economy. But Louisiana grew under 1 percent in jobs over a dozen years while the nation grew 11.5 percent. Depending on one boom-bust industry is the problem, not the solution.

Sources: The Data Center, 2026, LMOGA-commissioned study, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Offshore wind would never work in the Gulf

Rebuttal: The Gulf has weaker winds than the Northeast, so it's a harder case. But Louisiana won the first Gulf wind lease, and our shipyards and fabricators already build offshore. The leases ended in a $1.22 billion federal settlement in 2026, a political choice, not an engineering verdict.

Sources: RWE / Marine Log, 2026, Bureau of Ocean Energy Management

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Plugging old wells is the state's job, not the companies'

Rebuttal: The state does have a duty to act. But companies drilled more than 76,000 permits in coastal parishes from 1901 to 2017, and fewer than about 50 of 27,483 dry or abandoned sites were filled in. Those who profited should pay to clean up.

Sources: LSU, 2022, Louisiana Department of Energy and Natural Resources

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: BP already paid for the spill, so it's time to move on

Rebuttal: BP did pay a record settlement of about $20.8 billion. But a judge found 3.19 million barrels spilled, 11 workers died, and the biggest project the money was meant for was canceled in 2025. The public deserves to see that money actually rebuild the coast.

Sources: U.S. Department of Justice, 2015, Louisiana Illuminator, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Isle de Jean Charles shows relocation works, so we can just move coastal towns

Rebuttal: The New Isle gave families a safer place, and that matters. But it took a $48 million grant to move one small community. Moving whole parishes that way would cost far more than restoring the coast. Relocation should be a choice, not the default.

Sources: Houma Times, 2022, Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: People who live on the coast should accept the risk they chose

Rebuttal: People do make choices. But many coastal families were there for generations before the canals cut the marsh, and Isle de Jean Charles lost about 98 percent of its land since 1955. They didn't choose a sinking coast. Others chose it for them.

Sources: Houma Times, 2022, USGS, 2017

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: A just transition is just a way to kill oil jobs

Rebuttal: Workers have every reason to be skeptical; past promises to coal towns often fell short. A real just transition is the opposite of killing jobs: guaranteed wages, pensions and health care, and first hire on coastal restoration that already spent about $21.4 billion since 2005.

Sources: Louisiana CPRA, 2023, U.S. Department of Energy, 2025 USEER

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Climate activists don't care about working people on the Gulf

Rebuttal: Some climate messaging has ignored workers, and that's fair criticism. But the biggest costs of a failing coast land on workers: $5,400 average insurance, stalled flood projects, heat deaths. A worker-centered plan protects paychecks and homes together.

Sources: Climate and Community Institute, 2025, CDC, NCHS, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Environmental rules drive companies like Denka out of Louisiana

Rebuttal: Denka itself blamed compliance costs when it suspended LaPlace production in 2025. But the rules exist because EPA found cancer risk from chloroprene near homes too high. A plant that can only run by polluting neighbors isn't a business model to protect. Workers deserve a transition plan, not a choice between a job and their kids' lungs.

Sources: Manufacturing Dive, 2025, Chemistry World, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana can't afford flood protection without the oil industry

Rebuttal: Oil revenue has helped fund coastal work, and offshore revenue sharing matters. But the industry's own canals helped cause the losses being fixed. Asking polluters to pay their share isn't anti-business. It's paying your tab.

Sources: Minerals Management Service-sponsored study, 1987, Louisiana CPRA, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Hurricanes like Laura are just nature, and nobody could prepare for them

Rebuttal: The wind is nature. But Louisiana counted 25 deaths from Laura in about two weeks, many after landfall from generators, heat and cleanup. Those are preparation and recovery failures that policy can fix.

Sources: Louisiana Department of Health via KNOE, 2020, CDC, NCHS, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Building more levees alone will protect Louisiana

Rebuttal: Levees are essential, and the Master Plan includes about $14 billion in levee projects. But the plan also needs land building and about $11.2 billion for elevations and flood-proofing. Walls without wetlands get overtopped.

Sources: Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan, WWNO, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Rolling back clean energy credits will lower energy costs

Rebuttal: Removing subsidies cuts some federal spending. But wind and solar are often the cheapest new power to build. Forcing projects to start by July 4, 2026 or lose credits means fewer projects and less supply, which tends to push bills up, not down.

Sources: Kirkland & Ellis, 2025, U.S. Department of Energy, 2025 USEER

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Gulf residents who complain about pollution are against progress

Rebuttal: Residents want progress too: jobs, schools, roads. What they oppose is breathing exemptions. In 2025, 12 Louisiana chemical plants got two-year passes from new air toxics limits. Asking for the same protection as everyone else is not anti-progress.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025, EPA, 2024

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Citizens insurance is a burden on taxpayers and should shrink fast

Rebuttal: A big state insurer does carry risk. But Citizens grew because private insurers left after the 2020 and 2021 storms. Forcing families out before the private market is affordable just shifts them to worse policies or none.

Sources: Climate and Community Institute, 2025, Insurance Journal, 2024

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Sediment diversions never work

Rebuttal: Diversions are untested at the scale of Mid-Barataria, and that's fair. But the river built this delta to begin with, and the state's plan relied on land building because levees starved the marsh. Without diversions, the state needs a land-building plan just as big.

Sources: USGS, 2017, Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Federal disaster aid encourages people to rebuild in risky places

Rebuttal: There's truth there; some rebuilding is risky. That's exactly why prevention money like BRIC and elevation funds matter. They make rebuilding safer. Cutting them doesn't move people. It just leaves them less protected.

Sources: Congressional Research Service, 2026, Louisiana CPRA, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Fishermen and environmentalists will always be enemies

Rebuttal: The Mid-Barataria fight split them, and that's real. But both depend on a healthy marsh and a smaller dead zone. Shrimpers lose catch to the 4,400-square-mile dead zone. Common ground exists if plans pay fishers fairly.

Sources: NOAA, 2025, Louisiana Illuminator, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: We can just export more gas to fund Louisiana's future

Rebuttal: Gas exports bring money, but most profit flows to companies, not the state. Louisiana's poverty and slow job growth persisted through the boom. Without fair taxes, local hire and coastal funding written into deals, exports enrich shareholders, not parishes.

Sources: The Data Center, 2026, EIA, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The dead zone is the Midwest's problem, not Louisiana's

Rebuttal: The runoff starts upriver, true. But the dead zone sits in our Gulf and hits our fishers. That's why it needs federal action across the whole basin. The goal is under 1,900 square miles by 2035; we're far from it.

Sources: NOAA, 2025, Hypoxia Task Force

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana's insurance crisis is caused by lawsuits, not climate

Rebuttal: Litigation costs did play a role, and Louisiana passed reforms. But a dozen insurers failed after the 2020 and 2021 storms, and premiums still climbed. Storm losses drive insurance. Tort reform alone hasn't brought prices down to affordable.

Sources: Climate and Community Institute, 2025, Louisiana Department of Insurance

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Heat rules for workers will hurt Louisiana businesses

Rebuttal: Some businesses will face costs for water, shade and breaks. But heat deaths and heat injuries cost businesses too, in lost workers and lawsuits. 2,391 Americans died of heat in 2024. A few minutes of shade is cheaper than a funeral.

Sources: CDC, NCHS, 2026, OSHA heat guidance

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Climate change is real but Louisiana can't do anything about it

Rebuttal: Louisiana alone can't change global temperatures. But it can protect its people: fund the Master Plan, plug wells, fix insurance, harden the grid and train workers. Those choices decide how many people stay safe.

Sources: Louisiana CPRA, 2023, LSU, 2022

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Restoration jobs are temporary and low-paying

Rebuttal: Some project jobs are temporary, and pay must be fought for. But a 50-year, $50 billion plan is not a short gig. With union standards and steady funding, restoration can be a career like the oil field was.

Sources: Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan, U.S. Department of Energy, 2025 USEER

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Grand Isle should just be abandoned

Rebuttal: Grand Isle faces some of the fastest relative sea rise in America, around 3 feet a century. But it's also a barrier that shields inland marsh and towns. Giving up the island means more storm surge further in.

Sources: NOAA Tides and Currents, Louisiana CPRA, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The government overreacts to pollution near Black communities

Rebuttal: Every community deserves the same protection; that's all environmental justice means. EPA's own case said Denka's chloroprene risk to neighbors was too high. Dropping it in 2025 didn't change the air. Same standard for every neighborhood is not overreach.

Sources: Chemistry World, 2025, Manufacturing Dive, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana's coast was lost long ago, so there's no point fighting now

Rebuttal: A lot is gone: about 2,006 square miles since 1932. But the Master Plan estimates it can maintain about 310 square miles that would otherwise be lost and prevent around $11 billion a year in damage. There's plenty left worth saving.

Sources: USGS, 2017, Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Coastal Louisiana lost about 2,006 square miles of land between 1932 and 2016, roughly the size of Delaware

An area the size of a whole state, gone from Louisiana's map in one lifetime. That's homes, camps, fishing grounds and the buffer that slows a storm. A loss that big doesn't happen by accident. It took canals, levees and neglect.

Source: USGS, 2017

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
At its peak rate, Louisiana lost a football field of wetland about every 34 minutes

In the worst years, the coast vanished faster than a shift break. The rate has slowed since. The damage hasn't reversed.

Source: USGS, 2017

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's peak land loss rate was about 32 square miles per year, around the 1970s

The worst losses came when oil and gas drilling in the marsh was at its height. That timing matters. It points to who should help pay for the repair.

Source: USGS, 2017

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
USGS said the lack of a major hurricane strike on coastal wetlands from 2008 to 2016 was probably the main reason land loss slowed

The slowdown was mostly luck, not a fix. One big storm can undo years of calm. Louisiana can't plan its future around a quiet season.

Source: USGS, 2017

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
A federal study found canals directly caused about 16% of Louisiana wetland loss from 1955 to 1978

Canals were dug for pipelines and drilling rigs. They let salt water into fresh marsh, and the marsh died. That's a direct line from a business decision to a disappearing coast.

Source: Minerals Management Service-sponsored study, 1987 (via LSU, 2022)

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Canals and spoil banks together were tied to at least 30% to 60% of Louisiana wetland loss from 1955 to 1978

Count the direct and indirect damage and the industry's share gets big. Not all of it, but a lot. Fair is fair: those who cut the marsh should help restore it.

Source: Minerals Management Service-sponsored study, 1987 (via LSU, 2022)

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
There were 76,247 drilling permits in Louisiana's 14 coastal parishes from 1901 through 2017

That's more than 76,000 times someone was allowed to drill into or near our coast. Each one left a mark on the marsh. Together they reshaped Louisiana.

Source: LSU research, 2022

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
27,483 permitted land locations in coastal Louisiana were dry or abandoned by 2017, and fewer than about 50 had been filled in

Tens of thousands of holes left behind. About 50 filled back. The companies took what they wanted and left the cleanup to time and taxpayers. Plugging and restoring them could employ thousands.

Source: LSU research, 2022

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's 2023 Coastal Master Plan projects about 1,100 square miles of land loss by 2070 without action, and up to 3,000 square miles under faster sea rise

This isn't an activist talking. It's the state's own plan. The coast keeps shrinking unless we pay to rebuild it.

Source: Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Without action, more than 2 million Louisianans would face storm-surge flood risk and damage could reach $15 billion a year by 2070

Two million neighbors under threat and $15 billion a year in damage. Compare that to $50 billion over 50 years to fight it. The plan is the bargain.

Source: Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's 2023 Coastal Master Plan includes about $11.2 billion for nonstructural projects like home elevations, flood-proofing and buyouts

Not every protection is a wall. Billions are set aside to raise houses and help families move safely. Working families should be first in line, not last.

Source: Louisiana CPRA, 2023 Coastal Master Plan

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana spent about $21.4 billion on more than 140 coastal projects from 2005 to 2023

Restoration is already a real industry here. Dredges, pipelines, engineers and crews. Steady funding can turn it into the next generation of good Louisiana jobs.

Source: Louisiana CPRA, reported by WWNO, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana canceled the nearly $3 billion Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion in July 2025

The state's biggest land-building project was killed after lawsuits, a federal permit suspension and rising costs. Gov. Landry opposed it, citing harm to fisheries. Canceling a plan is easy. Replacing it is the hard part, and the land keeps sinking.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana had authorized more than $600 million for the Mid-Barataria diversion before it was canceled

Hundreds of millions committed, then the project died. The public deserves a full accounting of what was spent and what's next.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025
